uncertainty.method: Per-pixel change in dB (after minus before) after 9x9 multilook in linear power, minus the median change of all measurable pixels (+0.11 dB for HH). The no-change spread sigma (0.61 dB) is 1.4826 x the median absolute deviation of the change. A pixel counts as changed when its change is at least k x sigma and at least 2 dB, for k = 2, 3 and 4; patches that cannot hold a disk 11 pixels across are removed. Pixels within 1.5 dB of the estimated noise floor on both dates are excluded as 'cannot tell'.
notes: Each area is a range, not one value: low uses the strict threshold (4 sigma), central 3 sigma and high the lenient one (2 sigma). The sensitivity list shows how other processing choices move the central value.
HH: 23% of the area is at or below the noise floor on 2026-06-26, 12% on 2026-10-24 and 11% on both.
HV: 35% of the area is at or below the noise floor on 2026-06-26, 33% on 2026-10-24 and 31% on both.
The noise floor is estimated from the darkest part of each image, not from the instrument's noise record. Pixels at the floor on only one date are kept; their change is a lower bound.
Changed patches narrower than about 110 m are not counted, so thin features such as narrow channels or roads are under-represented.

caveats.text: 2026-06-26 is provisional-tier (calibrated, but values may change after reprocessing).
Wind roughens open water and changes its brightness from one pass to the next. A change over water is not by itself a change of the surface.
On steep slopes the radar image is distorted (layover) or blind (shadow); changes there are unreliable.
A change in radar brightness means the surface scatters the signal differently (water level, moisture, roughness, vegetation, structures). It is not by itself a land-cover label.

report.answer: Between 26 June and 24 October 2026, radar brightness rose over 0.26 to 0.48 km² (HH) and fell over 0.87 to 1.31 km² (HH) at the east end of Kamloops Lake. The nearby Thompson River gauge (8.4 km away) showed water levels fell from 4.992 m (26 June) to 2.313 m (24 October 2026), consistent with some areas losing water cover.
